entry: Semi-legendary medieval Indian tantric Buddhist master, also called Guru Rinpoche ('Precious Guru'). According to hagiographical sources, he fully revealed the [[Vajrayana]] in [[Tibet]] around the 8th and 9th centuries, and he is considered an emanation of Shakyamuni Buddha. Early Tibetan sources, including the *Testament of Ba*, state that he came to Tibet in the 8th century and designed Samye Monastery, the first Buddhist monastery in Tibet, during the reign of [[Trisong Detsen]]. Earlier Tibetologists questioned his historical authenticity, but Lewis Doney says it is now "cautiously accepted." From about the 12th century, hagiographies expanded his activities, and he is credited with concealing [[Terma (religion)|termas]], or hidden texts, for later discovery. The [[Nyingma]] school regards him as a founding figure and traces its [[Dzogchen]] lineage to [[Garab Dorje]].

Widespread, often global, [[Epidemic|epidemic]] of an infectious disease. A pandemic has a sudden increase in cases and spreads across a large region, such as multiple continents or the entire world, affecting a substantial portion of the human population. Endemic diseases with a stable number of infected people, such as seasonal influenza, are generally excluded. The [[Black Death]], caused by [[Plague (disease)|Plague]], killed up to half of Europe's population in the 14th century, and the 1918 influenza pandemic, known as the [[Spanish flu]], is the deadliest pandemic in history. Later pandemics include [[HIV/AIDS]], the 2009 swine flu pandemic and the [[COVID-19 pandemic]]. The [[World Health Organization|WHO]] Pandemic Agreement, adopted in May 2025, was approved with 120 votes in favor, 70 abstentions and the absence of the U.S., which had already withdrawn from the organization.

Prehistoric superocean that surrounded [[Pangaea]]. During the Paleozoic–Mesozoic transition, about 250 million years ago, it covered almost 70 percent of Earth's surface. Its original ocean floor has disappeared through [[Subduction|subduction]] along continental margins, and its layout is reconstructed from magnetic lineations and fracture zones in the western Pacific. The ocean is also called the Paleo-Pacific, because the [[Pacific Ocean]] is a direct continuation of it.

Act of stopping and disengaging a vehicle, usually leaving it unoccupied. Parking on one or both sides of a road is often permitted, though sometimes with restrictions. Countries and local governments set rules for the design and use of parking spaces. Cars are typically stationary around 95 percent of the time, and in many North American city centers, half or more of all land is devoted to car parking. [[Parking lot|Parking lots]] are either structured, such as multistory garages, or surface lots. In [[Park and ride]], people drive or cycle to a car park away from their destination and continue by public transport. The first public parking garage for motor vehicles in the U.S. opened in [[Boston]] on May 24, 1898.

American funk music collective headed by [[George Clinton (funk musician)|George Clinton]]. Its members rotated among the funk bands Parliament and Funkadelic, both active since the 1960s. Its albums *Mothership Connection* (1975) and *One Nation Under a Groove* (1978) received critical praise, and the collective had 13 top ten hits on American R&B charts between 1967 and 1983. Its mythology helped pioneer [[Afrofuturism]], and its work influenced later [[Hip-hop|hip-hop]] and [[Techno|techno]] artists. In 1997, 16 members were inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]].

Clade of ray-finned fishes in the subfamily Scarinae of the [[Wrasse|wrasse]] family. Parrotfish are named for their beaklike teeth, which form a tightly packed mosaic on the jaw bones. Roughly 95 species are known, with the greatest diversity in the Indo-Pacific, and they are herbivores or corallivores inhabiting [[Coral reef|coral reefs]], rocky coasts and [[Seagrass|seagrass]] beds. Some species eat away at corals, contributing to bioerosion and to the sand on the surrounding ocean floor.

Process of preserving foods with mild heat, usually to less than 100 °C (212 °F), to eliminate [[Pathogen|pathogens]] and extend shelf life. It destroys or deactivates microorganisms and enzymes that cause spoilage or disease, though most bacterial spores survive. The process is named after French microbiologist [[Louis Pasteur]], whose 1860s research showed that heating could deactivate unwanted microorganisms in [[Wine|wine]]. In 1768, [[Lazzaro Spallanzani]] showed that a product could be made sterile by thermal processing. In 1795 [[Nicolas Appert]] began preserving food in sealed glass jars placed in boiling water. Pasteurization is now widely used in the [[Dairy|dairy]] industry, and its mild heat causes only minor changes to nutritional quality and sensory characteristics. Non-thermal alternatives include high-pressure processing and pulsed electric fields.

American actress known for roles in film and television. She won the Academy Award for Best Supporting Actress for playing a single mother in the coming-of-age film *Boyhood* (2014), directed by [[Richard Linklater]] and filmed from 2002 until 2014. On television, she starred as a character based on Allison DuBois in *Medium* (2005–2011), winning a Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Drama Series. She has played Harmony Cobel in the Apple TV thriller *Severance* since 2022.

Theory and practice of [[Learning|learning]], most commonly understood as the approach to [[Teaching|teaching]]. As an academic discipline, pedagogy studies how knowledge and skills are imparted in an educational context. Its aims range from furthering liberal education to the narrower goals of [[Vocational education|vocational education]]. Instructional strategies are shaped by a learner's background knowledge and environment, as well as by the goals set by student and teacher, and one example is the [[Socratic method]]. The meaning of the term is contested, with the most common definition being the study of teaching methods, while some see pedagogy as an art or craft rather than a science.

Ceremonial capital of the [[Achaemenid Empire]], in [[Fars province]] of [[Iran]]. Its earliest remains date from 515 BC, and the palace complex, raised on a walled platform, served as the focus for governance and ceremonies. It appears to have been occupied only seasonally, and earlier most archaeologists held that it was used mainly for [[Nowruz]], the Persian New Year. In 330 BC, the army of [[Alexander the Great]] took the complex, and its wooden parts were destroyed by fire. One theory holds that Alexander deliberately set the fire to avenge the Persian destruction of Athens; another says it followed a feast at the urging of Thaïs, a courtesan, when Alexander was intoxicated. Exploration from the early 17th century helped lead to the rediscovery of [[Cuneiform|cuneiform]] writing. It is a UNESCO [[World Heritage Site]].

Anthropomorphized depiction of life's end, found in many religions and mythologies. In modern stories the [[Grim Reaper]], usually a robed skeleton with a scythe, collects the victim's soul. Other beliefs hold that death is a benevolent psychopomp, guiding the deceased to the [[Afterlife|afterlife]] without controlling when or how a person dies. Death is most often personified as male, but it is female in some cultures, such as Marzanna in Slavic mythology and Santa Muerte in [[Mexico]]. In [[Aztec mythology]], Mictecacihuatl ruled the [[Underworld|underworld]] of Mictlan as its queen. Death is also portrayed as one of the [[Four Horsemen of the Apocalypse]]. Most claims of its appearance occur in states of near-death.

Italian scholar and poet of the early [[Italian Renaissance]]. His rediscovery of [[Cicero]]'s letters is often credited with initiating the 14th-century Italian Renaissance and the founding of [[Humanism|humanism]]. In 1341 he became the second poet laureate since classical antiquity, crowned on the [[Capitoline Hill]] in Rome. His Latin epic *Africa*, about [[Scipio Africanus]], had earlier made him a European celebrity. In 1345 he discovered a previously unknown collection of Cicero's letters at Verona Cathedral. His sonnets were admired and imitated throughout Europe, and his vernacular *Canzoniere*, largely inspired by his unrequited love for Laura, established the Petrarchan [[Sonnet|sonnet]] form. He is also credited with developing the concept of the Dark Ages.

Species of [[Conifer|conifer]] in the family [[Pinaceae]], native to the Mediterranean region. Commonly called the Aleppo pine, it was named by Philip Miller in his 1768 book *The Gardener's Dictionary*. The [[Tree|tree]] grows 15–25 m tall, with orange-red bark and slender, yellowish-green needles produced in pairs. Its cones open slowly over several years, a process quickened by heat from forest fires. It is classed as an [[Invasive species|invasive species]] in South Africa.

Collection of anonymous Old Norse narrative poems in alliterative verse, also called the Elder Edda. Its poems are distinct from the closely related [[Prose Edda]] of [[Snorri Sturluson]]. Most are in *fornyrðislag* ('old story meter'), and about a quarter are in *ljóðaháttr* ('song form'). The collection's basis is the medieval Icelandic manuscript [[Codex Regius]], and its mythological poems include *Völuspá* and *Hávamál*. Like most early poetry, the poems were passed orally by minstrels before being written down, and their dating remains debated. Because Iceland was not settled until about 870, poems composed earlier must have been made elsewhere, most likely in [[Scandinavia]]. If its title is accurate, the poem *Atlamál* was composed in [[Greenland]] no earlier than about 985.

Sharp reduction in the size of a population, also called a genetic bottleneck. Such a reduction, caused by famine, earthquake, flood, fire, disease or drought, or by human activity such as genocide or intentional culling, lowers genetic diversity. The smaller population has reduced ability to adapt to environmental change, and inbreeding and deleterious mutations become more likely. A related form, the founder event, occurs when a small group becomes separated from the main population. Bottlenecks matter in conservation biology.

Capital and largest city of the Brazilian state of [[Rio Grande do Sul]] (pop., 2022: c. 1,400,000). The city lies on the eastern bank of the Guaíba Lake, where five rivers converge to form the Lagoa dos Patos, a giant freshwater lagoon. This junction made Porto Alegre an important port and industrial center. It is the southernmost capital of a Brazilian state and the capital of the [[Pampas]] region, home of the [[Gaucho|gaúcho]] tradition. The official founding date is 1772, though the village had begun in 1752 with Azorean couples. The city was the first to implement participatory budgeting and hosted the World Social Forum. It was a host city of the 2014 [[FIFA]] World Cup, having previously hosted matches in 1950.

Leader of the Powhatan Confederacy in the Tidewater region of Virginia. Known also as Wahunsenacawh, he led the main political and military power facing English colonists who landed at [[Jamestown]] in 1607. [[John Smith (explorer)|John Smith]] recounted in 1624 that Powhatan's daughter [[Pocahontas]] (Matoaka) kept her father from executing him, an account that many historians have doubted. By the early 17th century, the confederacy included about 30 tribes and an estimated 10,000 to 15,000 people.

City on the Warta River in west [[Poland]], administrative capital of [[Greater Poland Voivodeship]] (pop., 2023: 540,146). It is one of four historical capitals of medieval Poland, and it was a center of political power under the [[Piast dynasty]]. [[Mieszko I]], the first historically recorded ruler of the early Polish state, built one of his main gords in the city, and his baptism in 966, seen as a defining moment in the [[Christianization of Poland]], may have taken place there. The city is a center of trade, education and tourism, with about 130,000 students, and it hosts the Poznań International Fair, the biggest industrial fair in Poland.

Official review of events or actions ordered by a government body, also called a [[Tribunal|tribunal]] of inquiry. In [[Common law|common law]] countries such as the United Kingdom, an inquiry differs from a royal commission in that it hears evidence in a more public forum and focuses on a specific occurrence. [[Advocacy group|Advocacy groups]] often ask for inquiries, but governments grant only a fraction of the requests. Reports usually make recommendations and appear to earn public trust only when critical of government.

American filmmaker, actor and author. His works are characterized by graphic violence, extended dialogue with much profanity, and references to popular culture. He made his directorial debut with *Reservoir Dogs* (1992), followed by [[Pulp Fiction|*Pulp Fiction*]] (1994), which won the Palme d'Or at the [[Cannes Film Festival]] and his first [[Academy Awards|Academy Award]] for Best Original Screenplay. He later directed *Inglourious Basterds* (2009), an alternate account of [[World War II]], and two [[Western film|Westerns]]: *Django Unchained* (2012), which won his second Academy Award for Best Original Screenplay, and *The Hateful Eight* (2015). In 2021 he published a novelization of *Once Upon a Time in Hollywood* (2019), his debut novel. Critics have accused his films of misogyny and of insensitivity on racial themes, and he has countered that his protagonists have agency and complexity.

Indian actor, born Shivaji Rao Gaikwad, who predominantly works in Tamil cinema. His career began in 1975 with a debut in [[K. Balachander]]'s *Apoorva Raagangal*, and he has appeared in about 170 films in several Indian languages. His action film *Billa* (1980) gave him stardom, and *Thalapathi* (1991), directed by [[Mani Ratnam]], earned him major critical acclaim. The [[Government of India]] honored him with the Padma Bhushan (2000) and the Padma Vibhushan (2016), and he also received the Dadasaheb Phalke Award, India's highest cinematic honor. [[Forbes]] India named him the most influential Indian of 2010. His mannerisms and one-liners have earned him a large fan base.

Complex of 19 commercial buildings in Midtown [[Manhattan]], [[New York City]]. Its 14 original [[Art Deco]] buildings were commissioned by the Rockefeller family, and [[John D. Rockefeller Jr.]] developed the site on land leased from [[Columbia University]] in 1928. Construction began in 1931 during the [[Great Depression]], and the core was completed by 1939. Radio City, which includes Radio City Music Hall, was built for RCA's radio enterprises, such as [[NBC]]. Tishman Speyer has controlled the complex since 2000, and it became a New York City landmark in 1985.

Game in which players assume the roles of characters in a fictional setting. In the original form, the [[Tabletop role-playing game|tabletop role-playing game]], players interact through discussion, usually guided by a game master who sets the system and setting, while live action role-playing (LARP) involves physical performance. [[Dungeons & Dragons]], published in 1974, helped establish the modern tabletop industry. Players' choices affect the story, which distinguishes these games from traditional fiction and makes them a form of collaborative [[Storytelling|storytelling]]. Electronic forms include [[Role-playing video game|role-playing video games]] and [[Massively multiplayer online role-playing game|massively multiplayer online role-playing games]]. Tabletop games are also used in therapy, commonly with young people with autism or [[Dyslexia|dyslexia]].

Ashkenazi Jewish noble banking family originally from [[Frankfurt]], Germany. Its documented history begins in 16th-century Frankfurt, and its name derives from the family house. [[Mayer Amschel Rothschild]], a court factor to the Landgraves of Hesse-Kassel in the [[Holy Roman Empire]], established a banking business in the 1760s and installed his five sons in [[Paris]], [[London]], [[Vienna]], Frankfurt and Naples. During the 19th century the family possessed the largest private fortune in the world, and it dominated European finance from the 1820s to the 1870s. Its assets later spread across financial services, real estate, mining, agriculture and winemaking. The family has frequently been the subject of antisemitic conspiracy theories.

Granular material composed of finely divided rock and [[Mineral|mineral]] particles, usually defined by grain size. Sand grains are smaller than [[Gravel|gravel]] and coarser than [[Silt|silt]]. The most common constituent in inland and non-tropical coastal settings is [[Quartz|quartz]], a form of silica. Calcium carbonate is the second most common type, formed as aragonite by [[Coral|coral]] and shellfish, and it is the primary sand where reefs have dominated for millions of years, as in the [[Caribbean]]. Sand is a non-renewable resource over human timescales, and desert sand, though plentiful, is unsuitable for [[Concrete|concrete]]. About 50 billion tons of beach and fossil sand are used each year for construction.
